The proposed carpet cloak consists of a single-layer metasurface with 15 unit cells, each designed using the PSO algorithm in combination with a deep neural network.
The unit cell structure includes an E-shaped copper planar structure with a copper trace width of 0.4 mm, connected to the ground by two copper vias.
The substrate is Rogers RO4003C with a thickness of 1.6 mm, a relative permittivity of 3.5, and a loss tangent of 0.0027.
The unit cell periodicity is 6 mm, and the 4 tunable design parameters are the lengths of the E-shaped structure and the vias.
The deep neural network is trained on a dataset of 3,240 different unit cell designs and their corresponding reflection phases and magnitudes for 5 incident angles.
The trained neural network is able to generate the reflection phases and magnitudes for new unit cell designs in a fraction of a second, enabling the efficient use of the PSO algorithm.
The average reflection phase error of the 15 optimized unit cells is 4.03°, which is significantly lower than the 24.85° error for a design without the deep neural network and PSO algorithm.
The designed carpet cloak is numerically analyzed using full-wave simulations, and its performance is evaluated using near-field and far-field results.
The far-field results show that the designed carpet cloak can operate well for incident angles up to 65°, with the performance degrading for the 70° incident angle.

The Reduced Total RCS metric is used to compare the performance of the proposed cloak with a simple cloak designed for normal incidence, showing the superior wide-angle performance of the proposed cloak.

The use of longitudinal vias in the unit cell structure helps exploit the differences in the longitudinal electric field component for different incident angles, enabling the generation of diverse reflection phases.
The proposed design approach, combining a deep neural network and PSO algorithm, is crucial for achieving the wide-angle performance, as it enables efficient exploration of the design space.
The designed carpet cloak is fabricable using standard printed circuit board (PCB) technology, with the substrate thickness and via diameter kept constant to simplify the fabrication process.
The passive nature of the designed carpet cloak avoids the complexity, delay, and power consumption issues associated with active, reconfigurable metasurface-based cloaks.

The results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach in developing a passive, wide-angle carpet cloak, addressing the key challenge of incident angle dependence in metasurface-based cloaking.
